abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic paradigm for geometry processing that fundamentally rethinks how geometric information is quantified and manipulated. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on differential coordinates or spectral analysis, we establish a unified framework based on heat kernel theory and geometric entropy. The core contribution lies in defining a rigorous measure of shape information content through the spectral decomposition of the heat equation on manifolds. We prove that this information-theoretic perspective provides a natural multi-scale representation that simultaneously captures local geometric details and global topological characteristics. The mathematical foundation establishes deep connections between Ricci curvature, heat flow, and information theory that were previously unrecognized in the graphical models literature. This paradigm shift enables entirely new approaches to shape matching, segmentation, and correspondence that transcend the limitations of traditional geometric descriptors. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our framework possesses desirable properties including scale invariance, stability under perturbations, and computational tractability. The proposed information-theoretic paradigm opens promising research directions for geometry processing, offering a mathematically elegant alternative to existing methodologies.

We present a theoretically grounded improvement to rational B-spline basis functions that addresses the long-standing accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in NURBS surface fitting. The conventional approach of minimizing squared distance errors leads to oscillatory control points when approximating complex geometric shapes, particularly in regions of high curvature. Our method introduces a novel regularization functional that balances approximation accuracy with control point smoothness through a theoretically justified weighting scheme derived from the geodesic curvature flow. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees by proving that the proposed functional satisfies the Euler-Lagrange conditions with unique minimizers in appropriate Sobolev spaces. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approach achieves asymptotically optimal convergence rates while significantly reducing the oscillation artifacts that plague traditional methods. Experimental validation on benchmark CAD models confirms the theoretical predictions, showing average improvements of 35% in geometric accuracy and 50% reduction in control point oscillation for comparable computational cost. This work provides the first complete theoretical analysis explaining why certain parameterization choices outperform others, offering design guidelines for practitioners seeking optimal surface representations.

We introduce MeshForge, a groundbreaking mesh processing system that departs fundamentally from traditional pipeline architectures by adopting a constraint-centric design philosophy. Conventional mesh processing systems treat geometry and topology as separate concerns, requiring complex handshaking protocols between modules. Our system treats mesh entities as first-class constraint network members, enabling unified handling of geometric attributes, topological relationships, and validity conditions. The architecture employs a novel constraint propagation engine based on lazy evaluation and incremental dependency tracking that supports real-time feedback during interactive modeling operations. The core innovation lies in the hierarchical constraint graph representation that seamlessly handles constraints spanning multiple resolution levels, enabling operations impossible in traditional frameworks. We demonstrate the system's capability through challenging applications including guaranteed-injective deformations, automatic topology correction, and multi-resolution constraint enforcement that previously required specialized algorithms for each task. Performance evaluations show that the unified architecture achieves comparable or better throughput than specialized tools while enabling entirely new classes of mesh processing workflows. MeshForge represents a paradigm shift from specialized operators toward general-purpose constraint solving in graphical models.

This paper presents SubdivisionMesh Pro, a high-performance subdivision surface system that achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art implementations through innovative GPU-centric architecture and memory management strategies. Existing subdivision surface systems suffer from significant bottlenecks when handling models with millions of control points, particularly during adaptive subdivision and feature-preserving simplification. Our system introduces a novel streaming subdivision algorithm that exploits temporal coherence across animation frames, reducing per-frame computation by 60% compared to previous GPU implementations. The architecture incorporates a hierarchical buffer management scheme that minimizes GPU memory bandwidth consumption while maintaining cache-friendly access patterns for irregular mesh connectivity. We present a comprehensive feature-preservation framework that automatically detects and maintains sharp features, creases, and semi-sharp edges during subdivision without user intervention. The system achieves real-time performance for models with 10 million control points at 60 FPS on commodity graphics hardware, representing a 4x improvement over previous systems. Extensive validation through production use cases in character modeling and architectural design demonstrates the practical impact of our contributions to the computer graphics and CAD communities.
